# docs/index.md

# Extract

Extract reads PDFs, scanned or digital, on your own computer and gives you their text. Unlike plain OCR, it also tells
you which words and numbers are probably wrong, so you review a few flagged words instead of the whole page.

It is for people who need the text of a scanned letter, a council ordinance or an invoice and cannot afford a wrong digit
going unnoticed: finance teams, archives, anyone who feeds OCR output into something else. It comes as a local web
interface and as a Python library. If you write code against it, yourself or with an AI assistant, start with `AGENTS.md`
at the root of the repository: the calls for the common tasks, on one page.

## What it does

Every word comes out with a status. `ok` means the guard did not flag it, `doubtful` means it is probably wrong, and
`unscored` means nothing could judge it; words taken from the text layer of a digital page are `native`, and two more,
`fixed` and `absorbed`, appear only when corrections are on. A doubtful word carries its reasons and sometimes a
suggestion.

Every number is checked with rules, not with the OCR's confidence: the letter of a Spanish DNI, the check digits of an
IBAN, the arithmetic of an invoice. Only a rule that would break on any wrong digit can make a number `checked`. When one
fails, Extract says so and, if exactly one digit change would fix it, suggests that digit.

Nothing is changed behind your back. By default Extract proposes and you decide; if you switch corrections on, every fix
is kept with its reasons and can be undone. The result is a searchable PDF, a JSON file with every word and its box, an
Excel workbook and plain text. Nothing is uploaded: reading works with the network unplugged.

## An example

From the root of the repository, on a sample invoice whose total is 30 cents off (every name and number in it is
invented):

```python
import extract

if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf")
    for number in doc.numbers:
        if number.status == "mismatch":
            print(number.text, number.status)
    total = [n for n in doc.numbers if n.text == "101.913,81"][0]
    print(total.suggestion)
```

```text
# output
84.226,04 mismatch
17.687,47 mismatch
101.913,81 mismatch
DigitSuggestion(position=8, old='8', new='5', verified=True, rule='checks.rule.total')
```

The invoice prints a total of `101.913,81`. The lines add up and the VAT is right, so the total should be `101.913,51`:
the character at position 8 of the text, an `8`, would have to be a `5`. The subtotal and the VAT amount are `mismatch` as
well, because the total rule involves them. The [tutorial](tutorials/invoice.md) works through this sample.

## What it does not do

It reads PDFs only, in Spanish and English, with one OCR engine. It was tested on Linux with Python 3.10; Windows is
untested and macOS is not supported. It cannot confirm a number that has no rule, and `doubtful` is a likelihood, not a
verdict. [Accuracy and limits](accuracy.md) gives every figure with the conditions it was measured under, and every limit
with its reason.

## Where to go next

- New here: [install it](getting-started/installation.md), then follow the [quickstart](getting-started/quickstart.md)
  and the [tutorial](tutorials/invoice.md).
- Understanding it: [how it works](concepts/how-it-works.md) and [number checks](concepts/number-checks.md).
- Solving a task: the [how-to guides](how-to/batch-a-folder.md), or [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) when
  something fails.
- Looking something up: the [API reference](reference/index.md) and the [JSON format](reference/json-format.md).

More in the repository: `CHANGELOG.md` (what changed in each version), `docs/release-notes.md` (the long write-up of
each fix it lists) and `docs/MEASURED.md` (every measured table, with its method and intervals).

# docs/getting-started/installation.md

# Installation

This page installs Extract with one command, says what that command does and where it puts things, and covers a machine
with no network.

## What you need

- 64-bit Linux with Python 3.10 or newer (`python3 --version` tells you).
- About 1.5 GB of free disk and a network connection, for the installation only. Reading never uses the network.
- A few minutes: the installer downloads about 400 MB, most of it OpenVINO, SciPy and OpenCV. On a two-core laptop it
  took about 4 minutes.

| Platform | Status |
|---|---|
| Linux, Python 3.10 | The whole test suite has been run. |
| Linux, Python 3.12 | A clean installation, the offline bundle (installed with the network cut) and a read of the sample documents work and give the same words, boxes and statuses as on 3.10. Its test suite has not been run. |
| Windows | A lock file exists and the installer knows the Windows paths (`py scripts\install.py`, then `.venv\Scripts\python -m extract.ui`). Nobody has installed or run Extract on Windows: test it on your own machine before production work. |
| macOS | Not supported: there is no lock file. |

## Install

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/PabloMedinaBetancor/extract extract
$ cd extract
$ python3 scripts/install.py
```

The installer ends by reading a sample page and printing:

```text
OK: 100% of the printed words read

Installed. Start the interface with: .../extract/.venv/bin/python -m extract.ui
```

Start the interface with `.venv/bin/python -m extract.ui`, or go on to the [quickstart](quickstart.md).

## What the installer does

`scripts/install.py` uses only the standard library, so it runs before anything is installed. In order, it:

1. creates a private environment in `.venv` (on a system without `python3-venv`, it fetches pip from a pinned wheel);
2. installs every dependency from `requirements/<platform>.txt`, each wheel pinned by its sha256 and installed with
   `pip install --require-hashes`, so a file that differs from the tested one is refused;
3. installs the Extract package into the environment;
4. downloads the OCR models, 31 MB, and checks each against the sha256 in `models/models.json`;
5. builds the word lists the guard uses, about 50 MB in about 30 seconds, from the `wordfreq` package (they are not stored
   in the repository);
6. reads a sample PDF, to prove the installation works.

Its options are `--venv DIR` (the environment somewhere else), `--offline DIR` (install from an offline bundle, below) and
`--ci` (also run `pip check` and list what was installed).

## Where things go

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| The program and its dependencies | `.venv` in the repository folder |
| OCR models | The folders of `$EXTRACT_MODELS_DIR` if it is set, otherwise the `extract/models` folder of your user data directory (`$XDG_DATA_HOME`, or `.local/share` in your home folder) |
| Word lists | `src/extract/guard/data/` in the repository |
| The work folder: page cache, `job.log` and `corrections.jsonl` | For the library, `extract` inside `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` if that is set, otherwise inside `.cache` in your home folder. The interface always uses `.cache/extract` in your home folder. `Options.work_dir` and `--work-dir` change it. |

Extract looks for a model in each folder of `$EXTRACT_MODELS_DIR` (separated like `PATH`), then in the user data folder,
then in the `rapidocr/models` folder of the installed package. Deleting the work folder removes every trace of what you
read; [Privacy](../concepts/privacy.md) says what is written where.

## The models of the thorough mode

The default installation does not fetch the reader models of the thorough
[second reading](../concepts/corrections.md#the-second-reading). Fetch them once:

```console
$ python3 scripts/fetch_models.py --all
```

That downloads the three models the default installation leaves out, 169 MB in all. The thorough mode loads two of them
(84.5 MB); the third was a candidate that lost the comparison and is never loaded. Without them, asking for the thorough
mode stops with an `EngineLoadError` that names the missing file. `fetch_models.py` resumes an interrupted download, skips
files already present, and deletes a file and fails if its hash is wrong; its flags are on the
[command line page](../reference/command-line.md#scriptsfetch_modelspy).

## If the word lists are missing

Without the word lists, `extract.read` stops with an `EngineLoadError` that says so. Build them again with the
interpreter of the environment, because `wordfreq` is installed only there:

```console
$ .venv/bin/python scripts/fetch_models.py --lists
```

Under the system Python the script stops with `wordfreq is not installed`. With no environment yet,
`python3 scripts/fetch_models.py --lists --from-release URL.tar.gz` unpacks ready-made lists instead, with the standard
library only; the `lists.tar.gz` of an offline bundle is such an archive, and a `file://` address works. Their data comes
from `wordfreq` and is CC BY-SA 4.0; [Licence and credits](../licence.md) has the full credit.

## Without a network

For a computer with no network, build an offline bundle on a connected computer where Extract is installed, copy it
across and install from it. The bundle holds everything the installation downloads: the source, every dependency as a
wheel, the OCR models and the word lists.

```console
$ .venv/bin/python scripts/make_offline_bundle.py
```

It writes `dist/extract-offline-<version>-<platform>.zip`, about 390 MB, for the platform of the computer that builds it;
`--platform` names another: `linux-x86_64-py310`, `linux-x86_64-py312`, `win-amd64-py310` or `win-amd64-py312`. The target
needs the Python version of its bundle. The Windows bundles are built, and nobody has installed from one on Windows.

On the target, unzip it, open a terminal in the `extract-offline-...` folder it makes, and run:

```console
$ python3 scripts/install.py --offline offline
```

The installer installs every wheel with `--no-index` and `--require-hashes`, so pip cannot reach out and a wheel that is
not the locked one is refused, copies the models and the lists from the bundle, and ends as online, with
`OK: 100% of the printed words read`. The bundle holds the default models only: for the thorough mode, run
`python3 scripts/fetch_models.py --all --dir extra-models` on the connected computer, carry the folder across, and run
`python3 scripts/fetch_models.py --all --source extra-models` on the target.

## Check an installation

```console
$ python3 scripts/verify_install.py
```

`verify_install.py` repeats the whole installation in a temporary folder with nothing cached and reads a sample, which is
what continuous integration runs. `.venv/bin/python scripts/verify_install.py --here` only reads the sample with the
installed Python, and works with the network cable out. The test suite is `.venv/bin/python -m pytest`.

## Read the documentation as a site

The pages in `docs/` read well on their own, and they also build into a site you can browse on your machine. The site
tools are not part of Extract, so they go in their own environment, outside the repository:

```console
$ python3 -m venv ~/docs-venv
$ ~/docs-venv/bin/python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/docs.txt
$ DOCS_PYTHON=~/docs-venv/bin/python .venv/bin/python scripts/docs.py serve
```

The last command regenerates the pages that are built from the code, then serves the site at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`.

## Next

The [quickstart](quickstart.md) takes you from here to a first result. [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md) covers an
installer that stops with a network error or a missing model.

# docs/getting-started/quickstart.md

# Quickstart

This page takes you from an installed Extract to a first result, first in the browser interface and then in ten lines of
Python. It assumes you installed Extract as described in [Installation](installation.md) and are in the repository
folder. If you are writing code, or an AI assistant is, `AGENTS.md` at the root of the repository has the calls for the
common tasks on one page.

## With the interface

```console
$ .venv/bin/python -m extract.ui
```

Your browser opens on the Extract page. On a machine without a desktop, add `--no-browser` and open the address it
prints; the address carries a token that changes at every start, and the page refuses requests without it. Leave the
terminal open while you work: `Ctrl+C` there closes Extract.

1. On **Import**, type the folder that holds your PDFs and press **Browse**. For a first try, type the path of the
   `tests/fixtures` folder of the repository: it has three small sample PDFs with invented content. The interface opens
   only folders inside your home folder.
2. Press **Add** next to each PDF, or **Add all**.
3. Tick **Spanish**, **English** or both, whichever the documents are in, and press **Read**.
4. When the bar is full, press **Go to Review**.
5. On **Review**, yellow boxes are the doubtful words and red ones the numbers whose rules fail. `N` jumps to the next
   one, `Enter` accepts it as it is, `Tab` takes the suggestion when there is one, and `E` lets you type the right word.
6. On **Export**, choose a destination folder and press **Export**. A box at the top says how many files were written
   and where.

Each document gives four files:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `name.searchable.pdf` | Your original pages, with selectable and searchable text. |
| `name.xlsx` | The numbers, the invoice fields, the words to check and your corrections. |
| `name.extract.json` | Every word with its box, confidence and status. |
| `name.txt` | The plain text. |

An existing file is never overwritten: a second export of the same document writes `name-2.searchable.pdf` and so on, all
four with the same number. The [interface page](../reference/interface.md) describes each screen and every key.

## With Python

The same work in code, on the sample invoice whose total is 30 cents off. Every name and number in it is invented.

```python
import extract

if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf")
    for word in doc.doubtful():
        print(word.id, word.text, word.suggestion)
    for path in doc.export("out/"):
        print(path)
```

```text
# output
p1w11 Pelmuda None
p1w13 Esquilmar Esquivar
p1w4 F-2026-0498 None
out/mismatch.searchable.pdf
out/mismatch.xlsx
out/mismatch.extract.json
out/mismatch.txt
```

`extract.read` returns a `Document`. `doubtful()` lists the words to check, most doubtful first, and `export` writes the
four files above into `out/`.

The `if __name__ == "__main__":` line is required. The OCR runs in worker processes that Python starts by importing your
script again, so a script that reads at its top level stops with an `EngineLoadError`; [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md)
shows what that looks like. While the models load, RapidOCR prints `[INFO]` lines on the error stream: they are not
errors ([Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md#lines-that-start-with-info) says how to keep them out of the terminal).

`extract.read` starts the workers and loads the models for that one call. To read several files, use one `Reader`, so
that start-up is paid once ([Batch a folder](../how-to/batch-a-folder.md)). With no options, a read keeps its page cache,
`job.log` and `corrections.jsonl` in the work folder, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/extract` or `~/.cache/extract`;
`extract.Options(work_dir="work")` puts them in a folder of your own.

## The samples

`tests/fixtures` holds three PDFs, all scans, with invented names, addresses and identifiers that cannot exist:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `doubtful.pdf` | One page, an invoice stub of eight lines. It reads without any word to review. |
| `mismatch.pdf` | One page, an invoice whose total is 30 cents off. It has three words to review and a `mismatch` total. |
| `unreadable.pdf` | Three pages; page 2 is nearly empty and comes out `unreadable`, so the document is `partial`. |

Next to each PDF there is a saved reading, `*.extract.json`. Those files are prepared test data for the interface, not
the result of a read; read a PDF yourself to get a real one.

## Next

The [tutorial](../tutorials/invoice.md) follows the sample invoice from its doubtful words to the failing total and the
workbook. [How it works](../concepts/how-it-works.md) defines `ok`, `doubtful`, `checked` and the other statuses.

# docs/tutorials/invoice.md

# Tutorial: an invoice

This tutorial reads a sample invoice whose total is 30 cents off, decides its doubtful words, finds out why the total
fails, and writes the workbook. At the end you know what `doubtful`, `mismatch` and `checked` mean in practice. It takes
about fifteen minutes, most of it reading; you need Extract [installed](../getting-started/installation.md) and a terminal
in the repository folder.

The sample is `tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf`: one page, an invoice with four lines, a subtotal, 21 % VAT and a total. Every
name, number and IBAN in it is invented. The total as printed is `101.913,81`, and the figures above it add up to
`101.913,51`. `examples/invoice.py` holds this page in one script.

## Read it

```python
import extract

if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf", options=extract.Options(work_dir="work"))
    print(doc.name, doc.status, doc.doc_type, doc.locale)
    for word in doc.doubtful():
        reasons = [reason.key.rsplit(".", 1)[-1] for reason in word.reasons]
        print(word.id, word.text, round(word.p_wrong, 2), word.suggestion, reasons)
```

```text
# output
mismatch.pdf done invoice es
p1w11 Pelmuda 0.19 None ['not_in_dictionary', 'low_char_conf', 'neighbours_unusual']
p1w13 Esquilmar 0.12 Esquivar ['not_in_dictionary', 'low_char_conf', 'neighbours_unusual']
p1w4 F-2026-0498 0.04 None ['not_in_dictionary', 'mixed_letters_digits', 'neighbours_unusual']
```

`done` means every page was read. `doc_type` is `invoice` and `locale` is `es`, which means the amounts are written like
`1.234,56`. The read gives the three words that need a decision, the likeliest to be wrong first, with `p_wrong`, the
guard's probability that the word is wrong.

Run it with `.venv/bin/python`, and keep the `__main__` line: the OCR runs in worker processes that import your script
again. The blocks that follow continue in the same session. The `work_dir` option puts what the read and your decisions
write in a folder named `work`, so that you can look at it later.

In the interface, the three words are yellow boxes on **Review**: press `N` to jump to the next.

![The Review screen on a real read of the sample invoice](../screenshots/real-review-en.png)
*The sample on **Review**, as a real read draws it. The selected word is the subtotal, `84.226,04`: it is Mismatch because the total rule fails, although its own lines rule passes. The screen was read in Spanish only; the code on this page reads in both languages.*

## Decide the three words

All three are doubtful for the same reasons: none is in the dictionary, and the words around them are unusual. They are an
invented company name, an invented customer name and an invoice number, and nothing is wrong with them. To decide, look at
the word cut from the page: the picture at the top of the right panel in the interface, `doc.word_crop(id)` (a PNG) in
code.

The suggestion for `Esquilmar` is `Esquivar`, the nearest word in the dictionary, and the guard gave it a probability of
0.009 of being right: a suggestion is a candidate, not a verdict. The page says `Esquilmar`, so you accept the word as it
stands:

```python
for word in doc.doubtful():
    doc.accept(word.id)
print(len(doc.doubtful()), doc.word("p1w11").status, doc.word("p1w11").review)
```

```text
# output
0 doubtful accepted
```

The list is empty. The word is still `doubtful` and its `review` is `accepted`: your decision does not rewrite what the
guard said, it records what you decided. In the interface, `Enter` accepts the selected word and `Tab` takes the
suggestion.

Two other statuses matter here. `ok` means the guard looked at a word and did not flag it, not that
the word is verified: all 95 words of `doubtful.pdf` are `ok`, and its `doubtful()` is empty. `unscored` means nothing
could judge the word: page 2 of `unreadable.pdf` gives fewer than 25 words, so the page is `unreadable`, its 11 words are
`unscored` and listed by `doubtful()`, and the document comes back `partial` instead of raising.
[How it works](../concepts/how-it-works.md#statuses) lists every status.

## The numbers

Words are one half of the document. The other is its numbers, and for each Extract runs the rules of
[Number checks](../concepts/number-checks.md):

```python
from collections import Counter

print(Counter(number.status for number in doc.numbers))
for number in doc.numbers:
    if number.status == "mismatch":
        print(number.text, [(rule.key.rsplit(".", 1)[-1], rule.result) for rule in number.rules])
```

```text
# output
Counter({'checked': 13, 'unverified': 11, 'mismatch': 3})
84.226,04 [('number_format', 'pass'), ('lines_sum', 'pass'), ('vat_amount', 'pass'), ('total', 'fail')]
17.687,47 [('number_format', 'pass'), ('vat_amount', 'pass'), ('total', 'fail')]
101.913,81 [('number_format', 'pass'), ('total', 'fail')]
```

Thirteen numbers are `checked`: a rule that would break on any wrong digit passed for each. Eleven are `unverified`:
nothing contradicts them and nothing confirms them. Three are `mismatch`, and the three fail the same rule, `total`,
because it involves all of them: the subtotal plus the VAT should be the total. The subtotal also passes `lines_sum` (the
four lines add up to it), and the VAT passes `vat_amount` (21 % of the subtotal). A `mismatch` says that the numbers do not
agree. It does not say which of them is wrong.

The invoice fields of page 1 are in `doc.invoice`, and `doc.field_status` says how far to trust each:

```python
invoice = doc.invoice
for line in invoice.lines:
    print(line.description.text, line.amount.text, doc.field_status(line.amount))
print(invoice.subtotal.text, doc.field_status(invoice.subtotal))
print(invoice.total.text, doc.field_status(invoice.total))
```

```text
# output
Formación presencial 21.211,12 checked
Transporte de mercancías 37.468,86 checked
Consultoría de procesos 3.860,14 checked
Auditoría de seguridad 21.685,92 checked
84.226,04 mismatch
101.913,81 mismatch
```

All four lines are `checked`: for each, quantity times unit price is the amount, to the cent. In the interface the
**Fields** tab shows this table, and a click on a row shows the word on the page.

## Why the total fails

The rule keeps what it expected and what it found:

```python
total = next(number for number in doc.numbers if number.text == "101.913,81")
failed = next(rule for rule in total.rules if rule.result == "fail")
print(failed.key, failed.params["expected"], failed.params["found"])
print(total.suggestion)
```

```text
# output
checks.rule.total 101913.51 101913.81
DigitSuggestion(position=8, old='8', new='5', verified=True, rule='checks.rule.total')
```

The subtotal, `84.226,04`, plus the VAT, `17.687,47`, is `101.913,51`; the page says `101.913,81`. Extract offers a way
out: change the digit at position 8, an `8`, to a `5`. The suggestion is `verified` because the rule passes with that
change and with no other single-digit change of this number.

A verified fix says that the figures add up with that digit; it does not say that the digit is the printed one. Look at
the page:

![The total as printed on the page: 101.913,81](../assets/total-crop.png)

The page says `101.913,81`, so the OCR read it right, and the error is in the invoice itself: the sample's total is 30
cents off as printed. That is the case this sample was made for. Had the picture shown `101.913,51`, the OCR would have
misread a 5 as an 8, and applying the suggestion would be a plain fix. Here the printed value is the record, the decision
is `accept`, and with a real invoice you would ask its issuer for a corrected one.

## Apply the suggestion

To see what a correction does, apply the suggestion here. With a real invoice you would not: the workbook should say what
the page says.

```python
doc.use_suggestion("p1w75")
word = doc.word("p1w75")
print(word.text, word.original, word.review, word.status)
print(doc.field_status(doc.invoice.total), doc.field_status(doc.invoice.subtotal))
print(Counter(number.status for number in doc.numbers))
```

```text
# output
101.913,51 101.913,81 corrected ok
checked checked
Counter({'checked': 16, 'unverified': 11})
```

The word now reads `101.913,51`, and `original` keeps `101.913,81`. The rule `total` passes, so the total is `checked`,
and so are the subtotal and the VAT, which failed only because of it. Your decision is in the work folder, one line for
each word you decided:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

last = json.loads(Path("work/corrections.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()[-1])
print({key: last[key] for key in ("word", "original", "corrected", "action")})
```

```text
# output
{'word': 'p1w75', 'original': '101.913,81', 'corrected': '101.913,51', 'action': 'correct'}
```

The log also records the three words you accepted, each with its time. `doc.reopen("p1w75")` takes the correction back:
the word has the text it was read with again, and the rules run again on it.

## Export to Excel

```python
import openpyxl

path = doc.export("out/", ("xlsx",))[0]
book = openpyxl.load_workbook(path)
print(book.sheetnames)
for row in book["Fields"].iter_rows(values_only=True):
    if row[0] == "total":
        print(row[:4])
for row in book["Corrections"].iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True):
    print(row[:5])
```

```text
# output
['Numbers', 'Fields', 'Review', 'Corrections']
('total', 101913.51, '101.913,81', 'checked')
(1, 'edit', 'user', '101.913,81', '101.913,51')
```

The workbook has four sheets. **Numbers** lists every number with its value, kind, status and the rules, in words.
**Fields** has the invoice fields: `Value` is the number you decided on, and `As read` is the text of the page, which your
correction does not change. **Review** lists the words still to decide, empty after your three decisions. **Corrections**
has what you changed. `openpyxl` is a dependency of Extract, so it is installed.

## Next

[Number checks](../concepts/number-checks.md) lists the rules and says which numbers can be `checked`.
[Batch a folder](../how-to/batch-a-folder.md) reads a folder of invoices into one workbook, and
[Review doubtful words](../how-to/review-doubtful-words.md) does this review in a script.

# docs/concepts/how-it-works.md

# How it works

What Extract does to a page, from the PDF to the output files, and what each status it gives means. Read it before you
rely on a status in code: a few of them mean less than they seem to.

![The steps from a page of the PDF to the output files](../assets/pipeline.svg)

## From the PDF to the words

Extract first looks at each page without any OCR. A page has a legible text layer when it holds at least 80 non-space
characters, at least 80 % of them ordinary characters, and, if it has 12 or more words of three letters or more, at least
35 % of those words are in the word lists. Its words are then taken from the layer with the status `native`: nothing was
recognised, so they have no confidence and are never `doubtful`. Extract trusts such a layer, and a layer that looks
legible but differs from what is printed is not detected. `extract.inspect` tells you beforehand: `digital` when every page
has a usable layer, `scanned` when none does, `mixed` otherwise.

Any other page is read with OCR. It is rendered at the resolution of its own scan, taken from the widest image that covers
at least half the page and kept between 100 and 300 dpi; a page with no such image is rendered at 200 dpi, and no side is
longer than 3,000 pixels. A scan under 100 dpi is read at 100 and gets a page note with its real resolution, since nothing
in its words says whether it read well. Words come out in reading order, which follows the lines across the page, so a page
with two columns is read across both.

### Worker processes

OCR runs in up to two worker processes, which Python starts with `spawn`: each one imports your main script again. That is
why a script that reads keeps its calls to `extract` under `if __name__ == "__main__":`. Without the guard, the worker that
imports the script runs the read again and stops with an error on its standard error, the page comes out `unreadable` with
the reason `page.reason.render_failed`, and no exception reaches your code; [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md) shows
the symptom.

Each worker is budgeted about 1,500 MB with OpenVINO and 700 MB with ONNX Runtime, with 800 MB kept for the rest of the
system; with fewer than 600 MB free, no worker starts until memory recovers. A worker is replaced after 120 pages, or sooner
when its memory passes about 1.4 GB (a worker is checked only after a chunk of up to four pages, measured to add up to 190 MB, so that is 200 MB under the 1,600 MB bound of [Accuracy and limits](../accuracy.md#speed-and-memory)), so a long run stays as fast at the end as at the start. Digital pages and pages in the
page cache, keyed by the hash of the file, the page, the resolution and the engine, are handled in your own process: a
second read of a file with the same work folder costs no OCR.

### When a page cannot be read

A page is `unreadable` when fewer than 25 words came out, when the mean word confidence is under 0.65, or when it could not
be rendered or its worker died twice. Its words are kept as `unscored`, its numbers are never `checked`, and the document is
`partial`: it is returned, not raised.

## The guard

The guard scores each OCR word from the confidence of its characters, a lookup in the word lists of the languages you
chose, a character model and the words around it. The result is a status (`ok` or `doubtful`), `p_wrong` (the calibrated
probability that the word is wrong), the reasons, and, when it has one, a proposed fix. `p_wrong` is a better guide than
`conf`, the OCR's own confidence, because it combines that confidence with the rest.

How many words it flags depends on the review budget, `Options.review`: `fewer`, `balanced` or `more`. Each picks a fixed
threshold, set on the development pages so that about 3, 5 or 8 percent of their words are flagged, and words with digits
use a lower one. It is not a quota: a damaged page gets more flags and a clean page almost none. The guard cannot judge a
page of more than 5,000 words, nor words without a usable confidence; those words are `unscored`.

A proposed fix is applied only in a correction mode you choose, and the optional second reading reads the doubtful lines
again before the guard decides. Both are on [Corrections and the second reading](corrections.md).

## Invoice fields and numbers

If page 1 has an invoice title (`factura` or `invoice`, allowing for a misread letter or two) in its top third and at least
two totals labels (subtotal, `base imponible`, VAT, `iva`, total), the document is an `invoice`, and Extract looks on page 1
for the number, date, subtotal, VAT pairs, withholding, total, currency and the lines of the table. Each field is a cell
with its text and the words it came from, or `None` when it was not found: a field is never guessed. Only page 1 is read
for fields. Anything else is `generic`, and `Document.invoice` is `None`.

Every word with a digit then goes through the number rules, as does every IBAN, even one written in groups;
[Number checks](number-checks.md) says how a number becomes `checked`, `mismatch` or `unverified`. Last, `Document.export`
writes the searchable PDF, the workbook, the JSON and the text. It reads no page again and never loads the OCR models, so
an export after corrections takes seconds.

## Statuses

Every word, page, number and document carries a status that says how far to trust it.

| Word status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `native` | Taken from the text layer of a digital PDF. It was not scored: no `conf`, no `p_wrong`, never `doubtful`. |
| `ok` | Read by OCR and not flagged. It means "not flagged", not "verified". |
| `doubtful` | Read by OCR and flagged as probably wrong, with its reasons and sometimes a suggestion. |
| `unscored` | Nothing could judge the word: it was read with no guard (`Reader(guard=False)`), the guard failed, the page has more than 5,000 words or no usable confidence, or the page is `unreadable`. Extract does not present it as fine. |
| `fixed` | A fix of the guard was applied to this word, and its first text is in `original`. It appears only with `correct` set to `safe` or `more`. |
| `absorbed` | The word was joined into a neighbour or dropped by a fix. Its text is empty. Same condition as `fixed`. |

| Kind | Values |
|---|---|
| Page | `native` (the text layer was used), `ocr` (rendered and read), `unreadable` (its `reason`, such as `page.reason.few_words`, says why, and `error` holds the text of a failure) |
| Number | `checked` (a rule that would break on any wrong digit passed, and none failed), `mismatch` (a rule failed: some digit is wrong somewhere, not necessarily the one suggested), `unverified` (no verifying rule passed and none failed: not wrong, not confirmed) |
| Document | `done` (every page was read), `partial` (at least one page is `unreadable`; `doc.unreadable_pages` gives their 1-based numbers) |

![The six word statuses, what sets them and what changes them](../assets/word-statuses.svg)

A doubtful word is a likelihood, not a verdict: read it as "look at this". Flagging generously is what lets most errors
be caught, and [Accuracy and limits](../accuracy.md) says how many flagged words are really wrong. A word you already
decided is never touched by a fix, and `undo` returns a fixed word to the status the guard gave it. The interface calls
the guard the word checker.

## Your decisions: `review`

Accepting or correcting a word does not change its status. It sets a separate field, `review`, which is `None` while the
word is undecided, `"accepted"` after `accept`, and `"corrected"` after `correct`. The block opens `invoice.extract.json`,
the saved reading of a sample, made as [The samples the examples use](../reference/index.md#the-samples-the-examples-use) shows.

```python
import extract

doc = extract.load("invoice.extract.json", options=extract.Options(work_dir="work"))
word = doc.doubtful()[0]
print(word.id, word.text, word.status, word.review)
doc.accept(word.id)
word = doc.word(word.id)
print(word.status, word.review, len(doc.doubtful()))
```

```text
# output
p1w11 Pelmuda doubtful None
doubtful accepted 2
```

An accepted word keeps `status == "doubtful"` and has `review == "accepted"`, a normal state. `doubtful()` returns only
the words whose `review` is `None`, so the accepted word left the list because it was decided, not because its status
changed: test `word.review` to know whether a word was decided. `doubtful()` also includes the `unscored` words, after the
`doubtful` ones; for only the flagged ones, filter: `[w for w in doc.doubtful() if w.status == "doubtful"]`. And accepting a
word never makes a number `checked`: only the rules do that.

## Next

[Number checks](number-checks.md) explains how a number gets its status. The [data types](../reference/data-types.md)
page lists every field of `Word`, and [Review doubtful words](../how-to/review-doubtful-words.md) shows the review loop in
code.

# docs/concepts/number-checks.md

# Number checks

Extract checks numbers with rules, not with the OCR's confidence. This page explains what a rule is, which numbers can be
confirmed and when a digit suggestion appears. Read it before you trust a `checked` number or wonder why another is
`unverified`.

## The idea

A wrong digit in an IBAN breaks its check digits; a wrong digit in a line of an invoice breaks the sum. A rule is a
calculation that either passes or fails on the number as read, with exact decimal arithmetic and no confidence involved.
Rules come in two kinds.

- A **verifying** rule would fail on any single wrong digit of the number it covers. If it passes, the number is very
  likely right.
- A **plausibility** rule can only fail. It catches what cannot be right, such as a date that does not exist, and passing
  proves nothing.

A number is `checked` when at least one verifying rule passes and none fails. It is `mismatch` when any rule fails, and
`unverified` otherwise. A number on an `unreadable` page is never `checked`.

## The rules

| Rule | What it checks | Can confirm a number |
|---|---|---|
| `dni_letter`, `nie_letter` | The control letter of a Spanish DNI or NIE. | Yes |
| `iban_mod97` | The check digits of an IBAN. | Only when the national layout fixes every position as a letter or a digit |
| `iban_length` | The country code and the length for that country. | No |
| `cif_control` | The control character of a Spanish CIF, which may be a letter or a digit. | No |
| `line_amount` | Quantity times unit price equals the line amount. | Yes, when a change of one in the last printed decimal moves the result by at least a cent |
| `lines_sum` | The lines add up to the subtotal. | Same condition |
| `vat_amount` | The subtotal times the VAT rate equals the VAT amount. | Same condition |
| `withholding_amount` | The subtotal times the withholding rate equals the withholding. | Never confirms; see below |
| `total` | Subtotal plus VAT minus withholding equals the total. | Same condition |
| `number_format` | The number is written in the style of the document's locale. | No |
| `date_valid` | The date exists. | No |
| `vat_rate_plausible` | The rate is one of 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9.5, 10, 15, 20 and 21. | No |

Sums accept both rounding conventions, half up and half even, so a total that differs only by how a cent was rounded
passes. The locale decides how amounts are written, Spanish `1.234,56` or English `1,234.56`: Extract takes it from the
majority of the unambiguous numbers on the document, and falls back to the first language of `Options.languages` on a tie.

## Which numbers can be confirmed

`checked` is possible for Spanish DNI and NIE numbers, for IBANs whose national layout fixes every position as a letter
or a digit (Spanish, German, British, Portuguese, Dutch, Austrian, Belgian and Czech among others), and for the arithmetic
of an invoice. These stay `unverified`:

- A CIF, and an IBAN whose layout allows either a letter or a digit in some position (French, Italian, Swiss and others),
  even when their control passes: the control cannot tell a wrong letter from a wrong digit there.
- The withholding amount, because a document may print it with or without a minus sign. A wrong digit in it is still
  caught, since the total and the withholding rules fail.
- An amount written with a space as the thousands separator, `1 234,56`, which the OCR delivers as two words.

A VAT rate outside the list above comes out `mismatch`: a rate of 19 % or 22 % can only fail. The list is Spain's VAT and
the IGIC of the Canary Islands, which is a limit when you read invoices from elsewhere.

## A number that fails

On the sample invoice whose total is 30 cents off, three numbers are `mismatch`, and the same rule failed for each:

```python
import extract

doc = extract.load("invoice.extract.json", options=extract.Options(work_dir="work"))
for number in doc.numbers:
    if number.status == "mismatch":
        failed = [rule.key for rule in number.rules if rule.result == "fail"]
        print(number.text, failed)
```

```text
# output
84.226,04 ['checks.rule.total']
17.687,47 ['checks.rule.total']
101.913,81 ['checks.rule.total']
```

The subtotal, the VAT amount and the total all take part in the `total` rule, so all three are flagged. The rule found
`101913.81` where the subtotal and the VAT call for `101913.51`. `mismatch` says that a digit is wrong somewhere among
them, not which one. The [tutorial](../tutorials/invoice.md#why-the-total-fails) follows this case to its end.

## Digit suggestions

When a rule fails, Extract looks for a single-digit change that would make it pass. The suggestion is `verified` only when
a verifying rule fails now, passes with that one change and with no other single change, and no plausibility rule objects.
If two changes would both pass, there is no suggestion at all, and IBANs often tie because their check digits have few
possible values.

A verified fix says that the figures add up with that digit; it does not say that the digit is the printed one. Look at the
page: if it shows the digit as read, the document itself is inconsistent, the printed value is the record, and the
decision is `accept`.

With `correct="off"`, a suggestion is only offered, and `Document.use_suggestion` applies it as your action. With `safe` or
`more`, a digit is changed automatically only when all of these hold: the suggestion is verified, the new digit is one the
recogniser had among its alternatives for that position, you have not decided the word, and the word is not an identifier
whose letter could be the mistaken one. In `safe` the arithmetic rules stay suggestions; they apply only in `more`. No model
ever changes a number: a digit changes through these conditions or by your hand.

`use_suggestion` handles only a number made of one word, and when that word carries a suggestion of its own, it applies
the word's suggestion, not the digit fix. For a number written in groups, such as an IBAN in blocks of four, correct the
word that holds the wrong digits with `Document.correct`.

On the sealed test, none of the 519 numbers that came out `checked` on 60 synthetic invoices was wrong;
[Accuracy and limits](../accuracy.md) gives the conditions of that figure.

## Next

[Corrections and the second reading](corrections.md) covers what changes a word on its own. The
[data types](../reference/data-types.md) page documents `Number`, `Rule` and `DigitSuggestion`.

# docs/concepts/corrections.md

# Corrections and the second reading

Extract can change the words it is sure about, and it can read the doubtful lines a second time before it decides. This
page explains the three correction modes, what a fix is and how to take one back, and what the second reading costs and
gains. Read it before you set `correct` to anything but `off`, or when you want to know why Extract changed nothing.

## Three modes

`correct` is `off`, `safe` or `more`. It is an `Options` field and also the one option `read` takes directly.

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| `off` (default) | Nothing is changed. Every word stays as read, and the best fix is only suggested. Choose it when the text must match the paper exactly, or when you will review every flagged word. |
| `safe` | Applies only the fixes that almost never break a word. In practice that is the check digits of numbers (DNI, NIE, IBAN) and little else: on the sealed test it changed no ordinary word at all. |
| `more` | Applies the fixes with the best balance, without the precision floor that `safe` keeps. Choose it for large batches you will not review word by word, such as an archive you want searchable. |

On the sealed test, `more` removed 19.5 to 21.2 of every 100 wrong words in Spanish and 10.9 to 13.0 in English, depending
on the model. In English with the default model it broke 7.6 % as many words as it fixed, just over the 7.5 % limit set
before the test, a miss that [Accuracy and limits](../accuracy.md) reports with the intervals.

## What a fix is

The guard proposes fixes while it judges a page, and Extract stores every proposal with its reasons. A fix has an
operation: `text` (a different text for the word), `join` (two or more words become one), `segment` (one word becomes
several) or `drop` (a word is removed). It has a kind, `accent`, `case`, `accent_case`, `letters`, `punct`, `structure` or
`number`, the probabilities that the new text and the old one are right, and the modes that apply it. A proposal whose
list of modes is empty is only a proposal: no mode applies it, but `Document.fix_info` shows it.

Some words are never touched: any word you already decided, and protected tokens, which are words with digits, `@`, `/`
or `_`, and words with two inner capitals. When a mode applies a fix, the word it belongs to becomes `fixed`, the words a
join swallowed become `absorbed`, and the text before the fix stays in `original`.

## A fix, applied and undone

The three sample documents give no applied fix with the default settings. One setting gives one: reading `doubtful.pdf`
in Spanish only, with `correct` set to `more`. The page has the word `dias`, written without its accent.

```python
import extract

if __name__ == "__main__":
    options = extract.Options(languages=("es",), correct="more", work_dir="work")
    doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/doubtful.pdf", options=options)
    print(doc.mode, doc.fixes["applied"], doc.fixes["by_source"])
    word = doc.fixed()[0]
    print(word.id, word.text, word.status, word.original, word.corrected_by)
    fix = doc.fix_info(word.id)
    print(fix["op"], fix["kind"], fix["source"], fix["modes"], fix["applied"])
```

```text
# output
more 1 {'dictionary': 1}
p1w55 días fixed dias guard
text accent dictionary ['more'] True
```

One fix was applied, and it came from the dictionary. The word is now `días`, its status is `fixed`, `original` keeps
`dias`, and `corrected_by` says that the guard, not you, made the change. `fix_info` gives the proposal: an operation
`text`, a kind `accent`, and the modes that apply it, here only `more`. Take it back:

```python
doc.undo(word.id)
word = doc.word(word.id)
print(word.text, word.status, word.review)
doc.set_mode("more")
print(doc.fixes["applied"], doc.word(word.id).text)
```

```text
# output
dias ok accepted
0 dias
```

The word reads `dias` again, with the status the guard had given it, `ok`. Its `review` is `accepted` on purpose: an
undone word counts as decided, so `set_mode("more")`, which applies the stored proposals again, does not put the same fix
back.

The language is part of the reading. In the same session, with the default, Spanish and English together, the same read applies nothing:

```python
both = extract.Options(correct="more", work_dir="work")
doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/doubtful.pdf", options=both)
print(doc.fixes["applied"], doc.word("p1w55").text, doc.word("p1w55").status)
```

```text
# output
0 dias ok
```

With both languages on, the guard does not flag `dias` and proposes no fix, while Spanish alone flags it and proposes
`días`. Tick the languages the documents are written in, and no others.

## Undoing and switching modes

Proposals are stored, so `Document.set_mode` switches the mode without reading the page again. Any applied fix can be
undone, and the original text, id and box come back: `Document.undo(word_id)` for one word or its group,
`Document.undo_page(number)` for a page, and `Document.undo_all()` for the document, whose text is then that of the `off`
reading. An undone word is marked `review="accepted"`, so a later `set_mode` never applies the same fix again; the proposal
stays in the document.

If the planned fixes would change more than 8 % of the words of a page, none of that page's fixes is applied, and the
warning `guard.warning.fixes_withheld` says so. That much change usually means the page itself is the problem: a poor scan,
an unusual layout, or a language that was not selected. Review such a page by hand; `doc.fixes["withheld"]` lists those
pages, each with its share of changed words. A page whose language is not among the `languages` you chose gets no fixes
either.

## The second reading

The second reading reads the doubtful lines of a page again with other recognisers, and lets a dedicated model weigh the
readings before it proposes fixes. It is off by default.

| `Options(second_reading=...)` | What happens |
|---|---|
| `False` (default) | Each page is read once. |
| `"thorough"` | For each page with doubtful words, 16 lines are read again with two light recognisers and 40 zones with a deeper one, in a separate reader process, and the thorough guard model judges them together with the first reading. |
| `True` | The doubtful lines are read again, but the packaged guard model was trained without second readings, so it discards them and sends a `guard.warning.readings_differ` warning for each page that has some. The time and the memory are spent and nothing changes. |

Where the evidence supports a change, the thorough mode proposes a fix: joining two words, cutting one in two, or a
different text. It is applied only in the `more` mode; with `off` or `safe` the second reading changes no word and only
costs time.

```python
import extract

if __name__ == "__main__":
    options = extract.Options(second_reading="thorough", correct="more")
    doc = extract.read("tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf", options)
    print(doc.fixes["thorough"], doc.fixes["applied"], doc.fixes["second_reading_failed_pages"])
```

```text
# output
True 0 []
```

On this sample the thorough mode applies no fix, and no page lost its second reading. That is not a failure: the sample's
three flagged words have no fix that passes the thresholds.

The thorough mode needs its own guard model, `guard-thorough.model`, which ships inside the package, and two reader models
that the installation does not fetch: `python3 scripts/fetch_models.py --all` downloads them once, and without them the read
stops with an `EngineLoadError` that names the missing file. It also needs memory. The reader process starts only when
1,600 MB are free and is replaced when it passes its cap of 1,600 MB; without the memory it is skipped with a
`reader.skipped` notice, and a page that goes over the cap keeps its first reading and is listed in
`doc.fixes["second_reading_failed_pages"]`. A reader process that sends nothing for 300 s while a page waits is killed too, with the same result.

On 60 pilot pages, a fixed set of pages of the corpus, it added 2.95 s a page on average (5.46 s at the 95th percentile)
in a clean run on a quiet machine without the memory cap, and the first page of a batch took 17.6 s at the product's cap
while the three models load. On the sealed test, with `correct="more"`, it removed 1.64 more wrong words per 100 in Spanish
and 2.11 more in English than `more` with the default model, and in English it stayed within the limit on broken words
(6.1 %), where the default model was just over it. Choose it for documents where every word counts and time is not the
constraint; [Accuracy and limits](../accuracy.md#speed-and-memory) has the conditions.

## Next

[Review doubtful words](../how-to/review-doubtful-words.md) turns this into a loop. The
[Document reference](../reference/document.md) documents `set_mode`, `undo`, `accept`, `correct` and `reopen`, and
[Options](../reference/options.md) lists every setting.

# docs/concepts/privacy.md

# Privacy

Extract reads your documents on your computer and sends nothing anywhere. This page says what that rests on, what it
writes to disk and where, and how to remove it. Read it if the documents you read are confidential.

## Nothing leaves the computer

- Reading uses no network. The only downloads are the software and the OCR models, once, at installation (`install.py`,
  `fetch_models.py` and `make_offline_bundle.py`), and each model is checked against a published sha256. After that
  Extract works with the network unplugged, and a test fails if reading opens a network connection.
- One of the libraries Extract uses, OpenVINO, would send an anonymous usage event to Google Analytics each time it is
  imported. Extract imports it with that reporting switched off, and a test fails if it is ever reached. No document,
  page, word or statistic is sent.
- The interface, `.venv/bin/python -m extract.ui`, serves a page on `127.0.0.1` at a random port. Every request must carry
  the token printed when the interface starts, which changes at each start, and a loopback host name, or it is refused.
  It browses only folders inside your home folder, and it answers only on the computer that runs it.

## What is written to disk

| What | Where | When |
|---|---|---|
| One JSON file per page read (the page cache) | `pages/<sha256 of the PDF>/p0001.json` in the work folder | While reading. A cached page is not read again. |
| A log of the engine's decisions | `job.log` in the work folder | While reading. |
| Every correction, acceptance, undo and mode change | `corrections.jsonl` in the work folder | At the first edit, then at each one. |
| The files of an export | The destination folder you choose | On `export`. |
| The file `Document.save` writes | The path you give | On `save`. |
| A hidden partial file, `.<name>.partial-<pid>.<ext>` | The export's destination folder | Briefly, during an export. A failed or cancelled export leaves none. |

Extract writes nothing in the folder of the source PDF. The work folder is `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/extract` or `.cache/extract`
in your home folder for the library, and `.cache/extract` for the interface; `Options.work_dir` and `--work-dir` change
it. It holds the words read from every document, as the page cache, and the original and corrected text of every edit, so
treat it as you treat the documents themselves. Deleting it removes every trace of what you read, and the next read of the
same file starts from scratch; to keep a reading, use `Document.save` or an export.

## What is not covered

Extract does not encrypt anything it writes. The searchable PDF is written without the restrictions of the original: a
PDF with an owner password that restricts copying or changes is read like any other, and the new file is not locked, so
keep the original if the restrictions matter and do not share the new file as if it were protected. A PDF that needs a
password to open is refused.

## Next

[Installation](../getting-started/installation.md) says where each download comes from. [Licence and
credits](../licence.md) lists the models and word lists Extract installs.

# docs/how-to/batch-a-folder.md

# Batch a folder

This page reads every PDF of a folder with one `Reader`, exports each document, and writes one workbook of your own with a
row for each, with the invoice number and the total when there is one. It is for anyone with more than a few files to
read, unattended. `openpyxl`, which writes the workbook, is a dependency of Extract, so it is installed.

```python
from pathlib import Path

import openpyxl

import extract

HEADER = [
    "File",
    "Status",
    "Unreadable pages",
    "Words to review",
    "Invoice number",
    "Total",
    "Total (value)",
    "Total status",
]


def value_of(doc, cell):
    """The exact value of an invoice field as a Decimal: the cell holds the text, its number holds the value."""
    return next((number.value for number in doc.numbers if number.word_ids == cell.word_ids), None)


def row_of(doc):
    invoice = doc.invoice
    total = invoice.total if invoice else None
    return [
        doc.name,
        doc.status,
        ", ".join(str(page) for page in doc.unreadable_pages) or None,
        len(doc.doubtful()),
        invoice.number.text if invoice and invoice.number else None,
        total.text if total else None,
        value_of(doc, total) if total else None,
        doc.field_status(total) if total else "not found",
    ]


def read_folder(folder, destination):
    """Read the PDFs of `folder` in name order, export each into its own subfolder, and write one workbook."""
    book = openpyxl.Workbook()
    sheet = book.active
    sheet.title = "Documents"
    sheet.append(HEADER)
    with extract.Reader(extract.Options(work_dir="work")) as reader:
        for pdf in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.pdf")):
            try:
                doc = reader.read(pdf)
            except (extract.UnsupportedFile, extract.PasswordProtected) as error:
                print(f"{pdf.name}: not read ({error.code})")
                continue
            doc.export(Path(destination) / pdf.stem)
            sheet.append(row_of(doc))
    Path(destination).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    book.save(Path(destination) / "documents.xlsx")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    read_folder("tests/fixtures", "out")
    for row in openpyxl.load_workbook("out/documents.xlsx")["Documents"].iter_rows(values_only=True):
        print(row)
```

```text
# output
('File', 'Status', 'Unreadable pages', 'Words to review', 'Invoice number', 'Total', 'Total (value)', 'Total status')
('doubtful.pdf', 'done', None, 0, '2026-0042', None, None, 'not found')
('mismatch.pdf', 'done', None, 3, 'F-2026-0498', '101.913,81', 101913.81, 'mismatch')
('unreadable.pdf', 'partial', '2', 11, '2026-0042', None, None, 'not found')
```

This is `examples/batch_folder.py`; run it from the repository folder. Each document's four files go into their own
subfolder of `out/`. A second run exports each document under the next free copy number, and replaces `documents.xlsx`.

## One `Reader` for the batch

`extract.read` starts the OCR workers and loads the models on every call; a `Reader` does it once, on its first read, and
keeps the workers until the `with` block ends, even if a read raises. It reads one document at a time: do not call
`reader.read` from two threads at once ([Use Extract in a web service](web-service.md) shows a service). The
`if __name__ == "__main__":` line is required, because the workers import your script again.

## Partial documents and errors

A page that cannot be read is not an exception. The document comes back with `doc.status == "partial"`, and
`doc.unreadable_pages` gives the page numbers, counting from 1: page 2 of `unreadable.pdf` above. The other pages are
complete. The words of the unreadable page are kept as `unscored` and counted among those to review, its numbers are never
`checked`, and the page says why in `reason`: `page.reason.few_words` (fewer than 25 words came out),
`page.reason.low_confidence` (mean confidence under 0.65) or `page.reason.render_failed` (it could not be drawn, or its
worker died twice; `error` then holds the text). Decide what partial means for your batch: the script exports such a
document and its row says so.

An exception means the file as a whole could not be read. Every error Extract raises about a file, a model or a job is an
`ExtractError`, with a `code` such as `error.password_protected` and `params`:

| Error | Raised when | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `UnsupportedFile` | The file is not a PDF, or `load` was given something that is not a saved reading. | Skip the file. Images must be put in a PDF first. |
| `PasswordProtected` | The PDF needs a password to open. A PDF with only an owner password opens normally. | Skip the file and ask for an unprotected copy. |
| `EngineLoadError` | A model, a word list or a worker is missing or could not start. The message says which, and what to run. | Stop the batch: nothing will be read until the installation is fixed. |
| `ModelMismatch` | The guard's model does not match this version of Extract. | Stop and reinstall the version you run. |
| `SourceChanged` | The PDF changed while it was read. | Read it again. |
| `Cancelled` | A `CancelToken` was set. | Nothing is wrong ([Progress and cancel](progress-and-cancel.md)). |

The script catches the two that a file causes and lets the others stop the batch. Some errors are not `ExtractError`:
`FileNotFoundError` for a path that does not exist (a glob gives only paths that exist), `ValueError` for a bad option,
mode or format, and `OSError` for a file that cannot be written. The [errors reference](../reference/errors.md) lists every
class.

## Invoice fields

An invoice field is a `Cell`: the text as read and the ids of the words it came from, not a number. The `Total` column
holds that text, as printed; `Total (value)` holds the number, the one in `doc.numbers` whose `word_ids` are the cell's,
whose `value` is a `Decimal`, exact to the cent. `openpyxl` writes a `Decimal` as a number; do not convert it to a `float`
to sum money. (`openpyxl` gives numbers back as floats when it reads the file, which is why the output shows
`101913.81`.)

A field that Extract did not find is `None`, never a guess, and `doc.invoice` is `None` for a document that is not an
invoice: test each before you use it. `doc.field_status(None)` returns `"unverified"`, which would read a missing total as
an unconfirmed one, so the script asks for the status only when the cell is there. Fields are read from page 1 only, so a
multi-page invoice is not covered. A `mismatch` total keeps the printed value: do not book it before a person has looked at
the page (the [tutorial](../tutorials/invoice.md#why-the-total-fails) says why). `doc.invoice.lines` holds the lines and
`doc.invoice.vat` one `VatPair` for each VAT rate; the [data types](../reference/data-types.md#invoice-invoicefields) page
lists their fields.

## The workbook of each document

The export writes, among its four files, a workbook with four sheets. **Numbers** lists every number of the document: its
text, value, kind, status, the rules in words and the page. **Fields** lists the invoice fields with their value, the text
as read and the status, and exists only for an invoice. **Review** lists the words nobody has decided yet, with their
reasons and suggestion. **Corrections** lists what was changed, by you or by the guard. Status cells are coloured, and the
workbook holds values, not formulas. `doc.export(folder, ("xlsx",))` writes the workbook alone.

## Many files, little memory

A read starts up to two workers, each budgeted 1,500 MB with the default backend: on a machine with 3 to 4 GB, run one
read at a time with `Options(processes=1, backend="onnxruntime")`. Pages read before come from the page cache in the work
folder, so a second run over the same folder costs no OCR.

## Next

[Review doubtful words](review-doubtful-words.md) decides the words and the failing totals before you export.
[Progress and cancel](progress-and-cancel.md) reports how far a long batch has got and stops it.

# docs/how-to/review-doubtful-words.md

# Review doubtful words

This page reviews a document in code: it saves a reading, loads it back in a later process, decides the words and the
failing numbers, and exports. It is for a tool that puts a person in front of the words that need a decision, or applies
decisions that a person has given. In the interface, the same work is the **Review** screen.

Extract does not decide for you. A word is `doubtful` because the guard estimates that it may be wrong, and a number is
`mismatch` because a rule failed: in both cases a person looks at the page. The code below takes its decisions from a
table, `DECISIONS`, where a real tool would take them from a screen. The table accepts the total as the page prints it,
which is what the [tutorial](../tutorials/invoice.md#why-the-total-fails) recommends for a real invoice.

```python
from pathlib import Path

import extract

SOURCE = "tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf"
SAVED = "work/mismatch.extract.json"
DECISIONS = {"p1w11": "accept", "p1w13": "accept", "p1w4": "accept", "p1w75": "accept"}


def main():
    options = extract.Options(work_dir="work")
    doc = extract.read(SOURCE, options=options)
    Path(SAVED).parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    doc.save(SAVED)
    print("read:", len(doc.doubtful()), "words to review; saved", SAVED)

    doc = extract.load(SAVED, source=SOURCE, options=options)
    print("loaded:", doc.source, "-", len(doc.doubtful()), "words to review")

    crops = Path("work/crops")
    crops.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for word in doc.doubtful():
        (crops / f"{word.id}.png").write_bytes(doc.word_crop(word.id))
        action = DECISIONS.get(word.id)
        print(word.id, word.text, "->", action)
        if action == "accept":
            doc.accept(word.id)

    for number in doc.numbers:
        if number.status == "mismatch" and len(number.word_ids) == 1:
            word_id = number.word_ids[0]
            if DECISIONS.get(word_id) == "accept":
                doc.accept(word_id)
                print(word_id, number.text, "->", doc.word(word_id).text, doc.word(word_id).review)

    left = [number.text for number in doc.numbers if number.status == "mismatch"]
    print("to review:", len(doc.doubtful()), "- mismatches:", left)
    print([path.name for path in doc.export("out/", ("json",))])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```text
# output
read: 3 words to review; saved work/mismatch.extract.json
loaded: tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf - 3 words to review
p1w11 Pelmuda -> accept
p1w13 Esquilmar -> accept
p1w4 F-2026-0498 -> accept
p1w75 101.913,81 -> 101.913,81 accepted
to review: 0 - mismatches: ['84.226,04', '17.687,47', '101.913,81']
['mismatch.extract.json']
```

This is `examples/review_words.py`.

## Save and load

`doc.save(path)` writes the reading as a `.extract.json` file, with the words, boxes, statuses, numbers and your decisions
so far, and `extract.load(path)` reads it back in well under a second: it loads no model and does no OCR. `load` looks for
the PDF next to the JSON, under the name it was read with; when the PDF is somewhere else, pass `source=`, as above.
Without a reachable PDF you can still read, correct, save and export to `xlsx`, `json` and `txt`, but `word_crop`,
`page_image` and the `pdf` export raise `SourceChanged`, as they do when the PDF is not the one the reading came from.

`save` overwrites an existing file without asking: to keep a checked, never-overwritten copy, use
`doc.export(folder, ("json",))`. Pass `options=extract.Options(work_dir=...)` to `load`, as above, so that the log of your
decisions goes where you want it and not to the default folder.

## The words

`doc.doubtful()` lists the words that nobody has decided, the likeliest to be wrong first, and after them the `unscored`
ones, such as the words of a page that could not be read: nobody judged those, so the person checks them like the others,
or has the page scanned again and read again. Show the person the picture of each word, which `doc.word_crop(word.id)`
gives as PNG bytes, and decide it once:

| Call | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `doc.accept(id)` | The word is right as it stands. |
| `doc.correct(id, text)` | The word is wrong, and you have the right text. |
| `doc.use_suggestion(id)` | The word carries a `suggestion`, and the person agrees with it. |
| `doc.reopen(id)` | A decision has to be taken back. |

A suggestion is the guard's best candidate, not a verdict: the one for `Esquilmar` was `Esquivar`, with a probability of
0.009 of being right, and the right decision was `accept`. Show it next to the picture, and do not apply it unseen.

A decision sets `word.review` to `accepted` or `corrected` and leaves `word.status` alone, so test `review` to know whether
anyone decided. A `Word` is a snapshot: ask `doc.word(id)` again after a change to see it. `accept` after `correct` keeps
the typed text and turns `corrected` into `accepted`, and a later `reopen` then does not bring the OCR text back, which is
rarely what you meant.

## The numbers

A failing number is not in `doubtful()`: its words are usually `ok`, and the number is `mismatch`. Loop over
`doc.numbers` and show those whose `status` is `mismatch`, with the page and `number.suggestion`, the one-digit change that
makes the failing rule pass when exactly one does. `doc.use_suggestion(word_id)` applies it whether its `verified` is true
or not, so show `verified` too. A verified fix says that the figures add up with that digit, not that the digit is the
printed one: if the page shows the digit as read, the decision is `accept`, as in the script.

`accept` never makes a number `checked`, and `correct` does only when a rule passes on the new text. A number written in
several words, such as an IBAN in groups of four, has no suggestion that `use_suggestion` can apply, and a tie gives no
suggestion at all, which is common for IBANs: correct the word that holds the wrong digit with `correct`.

## What is written where

Every decision is appended as one line to `corrections.jsonl` in the work folder, `work/corrections.jsonl` here, with the
word, the original, the new text, the action and the time. The log is a record, not what `load` reads: the decisions
travel in the saved or exported JSON, so save or export after you decide, as the last line of the script does.

## Next

[Batch a folder](batch-a-folder.md) builds one workbook from many documents. [Corrections and the second
reading](../concepts/corrections.md) explains the modes in which the guard applies fixes by itself, and how to undo them.

# docs/how-to/progress-and-cancel.md

# Progress and cancel

This page follows a read page by page and stops one that is under way. It is for a tool with a progress bar or a Cancel
button, and for a service whose caller can go away.

## Follow a read

Pass a function as `on_event`. Extract calls it, in the thread that called `read`, with an event object at each step:

| Event | When | Fields worth knowing |
|---|---|---|
| `Started` | Once, when the read begins. | `pages`: how many pages the file has. |
| `PageRead` | After each page. | `page`, `status`, `words`, `doubtful` (the `doubtful` and `unscored` words of the page). |
| `Progress` | Right after each `PageRead`. | `done` and `total`: pages read so far, and pages in all. |
| `DocumentRead` | Once, after the last page. | `status` (`done` or `partial`), `unreadable_pages`, `doubtful`, `numbers_checked`. |
| `Warning` | Any time. | `code` and `params`: something the read noticed, such as `ram.low` when memory is short. |
| `Finished` | Last. | `status`: `done`, `stopped` after a cancel, or `failed`. |

Pages come back in the order the workers finish them, not always 1, 2, 3, and pages that are cached or digital come first.
Drive a progress bar from `Progress.done`, and use `PageRead.page` to know which page arrived. The
[events reference](../reference/events.md) lists every field and every warning code.

```python
import tempfile

import extract

SAMPLE = "tests/fixtures/unreadable.pdf"


def show(event):
    """Runs in the thread that called read, once for each event."""
    if isinstance(event, extract.Started):
        print(f"started: {event.pages} pages")
    elif isinstance(event, extract.Progress):
        print(f"progress: {event.done}/{event.total}")
    elif isinstance(event, extract.DocumentRead):
        print(f"read: {event.status}, unreadable pages {event.unreadable_pages}, {event.doubtful} to review")


def follow():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        extract.read(SAMPLE, options=extract.Options(work_dir=folder), on_event=show)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    follow()
```

```text
# output
started: 3 pages
progress: 1/3
progress: 2/3
progress: 3/3
read: partial, unreadable pages (2,), 11 to review
```

The read takes a new work folder on purpose. A page that was read before comes from the page cache, so a second read of
the same file in the same work folder sends its events at once and shows nothing worth following. For a test of progress,
timing or cancel, always give the read a new `work_dir`.

## Cancel a read

A `CancelToken` stops a read. Pass one as `cancel`, and call `token.cancel()` from any thread, or from the callback
itself, as here:

```python
def cancel_after_the_first_page():
    token = extract.CancelToken()
    seen = []

    def stop_at_the_first_page(event):
        seen.append(event)
        if isinstance(event, extract.PageRead):
            token.cancel()

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        try:
            extract.read(SAMPLE, options=extract.Options(work_dir=folder), on_event=stop_at_the_first_page, cancel=token)
        except extract.Cancelled as error:
            print("stopped:", error.code, "-", seen[-1].status)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cancel_after_the_first_page()
```

```text
# output
stopped: error.cancelled - stopped
```

The read raises `extract.Cancelled`, and the last event is `Finished` with the status `stopped`. A cancel is not instant:
the workers are told to stop, and the read returns within about two seconds. The token is looked at while the pages are
read, so a cancel that comes after the last page is too late: the read returns its `Document` as usual, and its last
event is `Finished("done")`. From another thread it is the same call:
`threading.Timer(0.5, token.cancel).start()` stops a read half a second after it starts. A token works once and stays set,
so make a new `CancelToken` for each read. `Reader.read` takes the same `on_event` and `cancel`, and the two scripts above
are `examples/progress_and_cancel.py`.

## What a cancel leaves behind

The pages that were finished stay in the page cache, in the work folder: read the file again with the same `work_dir`,
and only the rest is read. A cancelled read returns no `Document`, so nothing else is left, and a temporary work folder, as
in the examples, takes the cache with it. The interface keeps neither the stopped document nor its pages.

`Document.export` also takes a `cancel` token, but it looks at it only between formats: a format that has begun is
finished and checked, and the formats already written keep their names.

## Next

[Batch a folder](batch-a-folder.md) lists what else a read can raise. [Use Extract in a web service](web-service.md) puts
a read behind a request whose caller may go away.

# docs/how-to/web-service.md

# Use Extract in a web service

This page puts Extract behind a web service: files arrive in requests, one thread reads them, and each request gets its
answer. It uses the standard library only, and the pattern carries over to any framework. It is for a backend developer
who has to read PDFs on a request.

## The shape

Three facts decide the design:

- A read takes seconds a page, and the first one also loads the models. Do not read in a request thread: the request
  would wait for the models, and the next would start another read.
- A `Reader` reads one document at a time, and calling `Reader.read` from two threads at once is not supported. One
  `Reader` for the whole service keeps the OCR workers and the models loaded between requests.
- Once the reading thread has returned a `Document` and nobody changes it, any number of threads may read it at the same
  time. The methods that change a document hold a lock, but the methods that read it take none, so a thread must not read
  a document while another changes it. This service never changes a document after it returns it.

So the service has one thread that owns the `Reader` and takes jobs from a queue, and a `Future` that hands each result
back to the request that asked for it.

## The reading service

```python
import queue
import threading
from concurrent.futures import Future

import extract


class ReadingService:
    """Reads one PDF at a time, on one thread that owns the Reader. Any thread may call `submit`."""

    def __init__(self, options=None):
        self._jobs = queue.Queue()
        self._thread = threading.Thread(target=self._run, args=(options,), name="extract-reader")
        self._thread.start()

    def submit(self, path):
        """Queue `path` and return a Future whose result is the Document, or whose exception is what the read raised."""
        future = Future()
        self._jobs.put((path, future))
        return future

    def close(self):
        """Finish the jobs already queued, then stop the Reader and its workers."""
        self._jobs.put(None)
        self._thread.join()

    def _run(self, options):
        with extract.Reader(options) as reader:
            while (job := self._jobs.get()) is not None:
                path, future = job
                try:
                    future.set_result(reader.read(path))
                except BaseException as error:  # the waiting request thread re-raises it
                    future.set_exception(error)
```

`submit` returns at once. `future.result(timeout=...)` blocks the caller until the read is done and returns the
`Document`, or raises what the read raised. Jobs run in the order they arrive. `close` puts a marker at the end of the
queue, so the jobs already queued are finished first, and then stops the `Reader` and its worker processes: call it when
the service shuts down. Creating the service starts a thread and loads nothing, but create it under
`if __name__ == "__main__":`, as below, because the worker processes import your main script.

## A request handler

This handler receives a PDF in the body of a POST, writes it to a temporary folder, asks the service to read it, and
answers with JSON. A file that is not a PDF, or that needs a password, is the caller's mistake, and the answer says so with
the error's `code`.

```python
import json
import tempfile
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler
from pathlib import Path


def summary(doc):
    """What the service answers for a document."""
    return {
        "status": doc.status,
        "unreadable_pages": list(doc.unreadable_pages),
        "to_review": [{"id": word.id, "text": word.text, "suggestion": word.suggestion} for word in doc.doubtful()],
        "numbers": {
            status: sum(1 for number in doc.numbers if number.status == status)
            for status in ("checked", "mismatch", "unverified")
        },
    }


def make_handler(service):
    class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def do_POST(self):
            body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))
            with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
                path = Path(folder) / "upload.pdf"
                path.write_bytes(body)
                try:
                    answer, code = summary(service.submit(path).result(timeout=300)), 200
                except (extract.UnsupportedFile, extract.PasswordProtected) as error:
                    answer, code = {"error": error.code}, 422
            data = json.dumps(answer).encode()
            self.send_response(code)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(data)

        def log_message(self, *args):
            pass

    return Handler
```

The temporary folder lives until the answer is built, because a `Document` needs its PDF for the picture of a word and
for the searchable PDF. `summary` only reads the `Document`, which the reading thread never touches again. Any error other
than a bad upload, an `EngineLoadError` or a full disk, is the service's fault and should reach your error logging as a
500.

## Try it

The whole script starts the server on a free local port, posts the sample invoice and a file that is not a PDF, and
stops:

```python
from http.server import ThreadingHTTPServer
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def post(url, body):
    try:
        with urlopen(Request(url, data=body, method="POST")) as response:
            return response.status, json.load(response)
    except HTTPError as error:
        return error.code, json.load(error)


def main():
    service = ReadingService()
    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), make_handler(service))
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/"
    try:
        code, answer = post(url, Path("tests/fixtures/mismatch.pdf").read_bytes())
        print(code, answer["status"], [word["id"] for word in answer["to_review"]], answer["numbers"])
        code, answer = post(url, b"this is not a PDF")
        print(code, answer)
    finally:
        server.shutdown()
        service.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```text
# output
200 done ['p1w11', 'p1w13', 'p1w4'] {'checked': 13, 'mismatch': 3, 'unverified': 11}
```
